config.yaml:
schema_version: 2

runtime:
  name: engineering-runtime
  log_level: info

# Optional Engineering Runtime Control Plane. When disabled (default), the
# runtime never contacts a portal — Community / local use stays offline.
# Enable only after an Enterprise administrator issues this installation a
# show-once Runtime Portal key.
#
# `engrt portal register` verifies and atomically installs the first signed
# policy/config generation, then permanently selects Enterprise authority for
# this Runtime Home. Later `engrt portal sync` refreshes that complete
# generation. A portal outage preserves the last verified generation.
#
# Env overrides: ENGRT_PORTAL_ENABLED, ENGRT_PORTAL_BASE_URL,
# ENGRT_PORTAL_PATH_PREFIX, ENGRT_PORTAL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS.
# Contract: docs/control-plane/API-v1.md
portal:
  enabled: false
  base_url: "" # e.g. http://localhost:8081 or your HTTPS Control Plane URL
  # The Runtime client accepts only the authenticated Enterprise v1 prefix.
  path_prefix: /api/v1
  # Bounds registration, manual sync, and at-most-once-per-process heartbeat.
  timeout_seconds: 5

# Authority is resolved independently of the caller. GitHub may use a separate
# ENGRT OAuth session in the OS secure store, or an explicitly selected input.
# Native gh remains independently authenticated. No token is returned to callers.
# Optional execution.surface: local | ci | kubernetes (omitted means undeclared).
# Observations restrict sources/prompts; they never select an identity.
# execution:
#   surface: local
authentication:
  provider: github

  github:
    enabled: true
    base_url: https://api.github.com
    token_env: ENGRT_GITHUB_TOKEN
    # source: os_secure_store # or github_actions | github_app | file | env
    # With source omitted, exactly one explicit token/token-file/JSON-file input
    # wins, otherwise use the host's ENGRT session. Multiple inputs refuse.
    # oauth_client_id: <owned-device-flow-client-id> # nonsecret; explicit login
    # mechanism: user_token # optional; installation_token for installation authority
    # app_id: "123" # github_app only; private key supplied separately
    # installation_id: "456"
    # ca_bundle: /absolute/path/to/company-ca.pem # extends system roots; no TLS bypass

  # Native CLI access tokens, not generic ADC. Token-info proof asserts identity
  # only when a stable subject is returned; otherwise readiness remains explicit.
  # Only explicit local terminal login may offer a confirmed gcloud auth login.
  gcp:
    enabled: false
    binary: gcloud
    # python: /absolute/path/to/python3 # pinned and version checked; ignores ambient CLOUDSDK_PYTHON
    source: native # native | credential_file | gke_metadata (no automatic fallback)
    workload_service_account: "" # exact mapped GSA email required in gke_metadata mode

  # Configuration readiness only: kubeconfig inspection is not API auth.
  kubernetes:
    enabled: false
    source: kubeconfig # kubeconfig | in_cluster; explicit, never inferred from CI markers
    kubeconfig_path: "" # defaults to $KUBECONFIG or ~/.kube/config

  # Validated via `oc whoami`. Enable once `oc login` has been run.
  openshift:
    enabled: false
    binary: oc
    server: ""

# Capability definitions live outside Runtime Home, because they are your
# engineering knowledge rather than Runtime's state.
#
# The usual setup needs nothing here: point ENGRT_CAPABILITIES_DIR at a
# directory and it is both where capabilities are read from and where new ones
# are written. Runtime never fetches, creates, commits or publishes it — you
# clone and pull it yourself.
#
# Sources below are for running several directories at once; they are searched in
# order and the first to provide a name wins. With more than one directory
# configured, name the one you author into with authoring_source — Runtime asks
# rather than guessing where your work should land.
capabilities:
  sources: []
  #   - name: team
  #     dir: /absolute/path/to/team/capabilities
  #   - name: personal
  #     dir: /absolute/path/to/your/capabilities
  # authoring_source: personal

# Maps an `engrt command run <binary>` binary to the Auth Engine provider
# it should validate against before executing. A binary with no entry here
# skips the Auth Engine entirely (it's assumed to manage its own
# credentials, e.g. terraform's provider blocks).
command_providers:
  gh: github
  gcloud: gcp
  gsutil: gcp
  bq: gcp
  kubectl: kubernetes
  oc: openshift
  # helm/flux/istioctl all read the same active kubeconfig context kubectl
  # does, and loginKubernetes() validates that file directly — no CLI
  # dependency — so the same check applies regardless of which of these
  # four tools is asking.
  helm: kubernetes
  flux: kubernetes
  istioctl: kubernetes

policy.yaml:
# Declarative policy is evaluated before every operation executes and composes
# with the non-disableable safety profile compiled into the Runtime binary.
schema_version: 3

# Provider Governance for `engrt <provider> <operation>`, e.g.
# `engrt github repo list`.
#
# Operations are discovered from the Provider that owns them, not from a
# list here — so a provider with no entry below can run every operation it
# exposes, and gaining a new operation never requires a policy edit.
# Governance is expressed as denials; add `allowed` to lock a provider down
# to an explicit set instead.
#
# Rules match by prefix against "<operation> <args...>", so a rule can deny
# a whole operation ("files delete") or one narrow case
# ("workflow run deploy-prod.yml", "api DELETE"). A rule naming an operation
# no provider exposes governs nothing — `engrt config validate` reports
# any such dead rule.
#
# Rules are evaluated on the operation, never on the transport the provider
# chose — a denial cannot be sidestepped by a provider moving an operation
# from REST to the CLI. When a provider does pick the CLI, allowed_binaries
# and command_policy below still apply on top of this.
providers:
  github:
    enabled: true
    denied:
      # The `api` escape hatch can reach any REST endpoint, including
      # destructive ones the curated operations deliberately don't expose
      # (there is no `repo delete` operation, and this is why one isn't
      # needed). Denying the DELETE method closes that path without
      # restricting the read/create operations above it.
      #
      # Rules are prefix-matched against "<operation> <args...>", so a rule
      # naming an operation no provider offers governs nothing. `runtime
      # config validate` reports any such dead rule.
      - api DELETE
  files:
    enabled: true
    denied:
      - delete

# File Engine governance for `engrt files <operation> <path>`.
#
# File access is default-deny: a policy document with no `file_policy` block
# grants nothing, and every read, list, structured edit, write, append and
# delete is refused.
# That is a deliberate change from the engine this replaced, which permitted
# every read anywhere on the machine and every write outside a short list of
# names inside the Runtime Home.
#
# Read and write are separate grants. A root in `read_roots` permits read and
# list; a root in `write_roots` permits write, append and delete. Neither
# implies the other, so a capability that summarises files cannot also replace
# them by virtue of being allowed to look.
#
# "." is the working directory Runtime was invoked from, resolved once per
# request. It is the default because it is the operator's explicit place of
# work — narrow it to an absolute path, or list several, when a fleet should
# only ever touch one tree.
#
# Some files are refused inside any granted root and cannot be granted by any
# document: Runtime's own configuration, policy, evidence journal and trust
# state wherever they were selected from, and the native credential stores
# adapters authenticate with (~/.ssh, ~/.kube, ~/.aws, ~/.config/gcloud and
# the rest). The refusal follows the file, not the name, so moving one or
# reaching it through a link does not make it readable.
file_policy:
  read_roots:
    - "."
  write_roots:
    - "."

  # Budgets bound what one operation may return or edit. These may only be narrowed by
  # a document — a value larger than the compiled bound is ignored, because a
  # limit a document can raise is a default rather than a limit.
  max_read_bytes: 1048576
  max_list_entries: 1000
  max_depth: 32
  max_edit_files: 1000
  max_edit_batch_bytes: 33554432
  max_edit_matches: 10000
  max_edit_diff_bytes: 1048576
  max_edit_seconds: 30

# Binary Governance for `engrt command run <binary>`. Only these binaries
# may execute at all.
allowed_binaries:
  - gh
  - git
  - terraform
  - gcloud
  - kubectl
  - oc
  - aws
  - az
  - vault
  - helm
  - flux
  - gsutil
  - bq
  - docker
  - podman
  - kustomize
  - argocd
  - istioctl
  - pulumi
  - packer
  - sops

# Subcommand-level Binary Governance, evaluated before Runtime Context
# injection so a denial can never be bypassed by an injected flag.
command_policy:
  # Refused outright even if they were ever added to allowed_binaries.
  denied_binaries:
    - rm
    - sudo
    - chmod
    - curl
    - wget
    - ssh

  # Per-binary subcommand allow/deny lists, matched against the raw
  # (pre-context-injection) arguments. A `denied` rule matches a contiguous
  # run of argument tokens ANYWHERE in the command, so a leading global flag
  # cannot bypass it. `allowed` rules match as a prefix. Denials always win.
  rules:
    # git can rewrite or discard history and push anywhere. Reads, commits
    # and ordinary pushes are allowed; irreversible operations are refused.
    # Rules match a contiguous run of argument tokens anywhere in the
    # command, so `git -C <dir> push --force` is caught exactly like the
    # bare `git push --force`.
    git:
      denied:
        - push --force
        - push -f
        - reset --hard
        - clean -fd
        - filter-branch
        - update-ref -d
    terraform:
      denied:
        - destroy
    gcloud:
      denied:
        - projects delete
        - iam service-accounts delete
    kubectl:
      denied:
        - delete namespace
    oc:
      denied:
        - delete project
    # AWS CLI: credential/account and bulk-data deletion are irreversible;
    # ordinary describe/list/get calls are unaffected.
    aws:
      denied:
        - s3 rb --force
        - ec2 terminate-instances
        - iam delete-user
        - rds delete-db-instance
    # Azure CLI: mirrors aws above — resource and identity deletion refused,
    # reads and ordinary management calls allowed.
    az:
      denied:
        - vm delete
        - group delete
        - ad user delete
        - keyvault delete
    # Vault: refuses permanent secret/engine removal. Sealing/unsealing and
    # token operations are intentionally not denied here — they are not data
    # loss, just availability, and are already gated by Vault's own ACLs.
    vault:
      denied:
        - kv delete
        - kv metadata delete
        - secrets disable
    # Helm: uninstall tears down an entire release (the closest equivalent
    # to terraform's destroy), so it is denied outright like destroy is.
    helm:
      denied:
        - uninstall
    # Flux: delete/uninstall remove GitOps-managed resources or Flux itself
    # from the cluster; suspend/resume and get/diff are unaffected.
    flux:
      denied:
        - delete
        - uninstall
    # gsutil (SDK membership does not establish a native auth contract): recursive object
    # deletion and bucket removal are irreversible; cp/mv/ls/cat are not.
    gsutil:
      denied:
        - rm -r
        - rb
    # bq (also gcloud SDK): -f skips the interactive confirmation prompt
    # rm would otherwise show, for both a table and a whole dataset — denied
    # in both flag orders since -r (recursive/dataset) can precede -f.
    bq:
      denied:
        - rm -f
        - rm -r -f
        - rm -f -r
    # Docker: bulk pruning and force-removal are irreversible; run
    # --privileged is denied as a container-escape risk, not a deletion one.
    docker:
      denied:
        - system prune -a
        - volume rm
        - network rm
        - run --privileged
    # Podman: same daemon-less CLI, same risks as docker above.
    podman:
      denied:
        - system prune -a
        - volume rm
        - run --privileged
    # kustomize only renders YAML to stdout — it never talks to a cluster or
    # registry itself (that's kubectl's job), so no denial rule is needed.
    # Argo CD: app/cluster/repo removal detaches or deletes GitOps-managed
    # state; sync/diff/get and ordinary app management are unaffected.
    argocd:
      denied:
        - app delete
        - cluster rm
        - repo rm
    # istioctl: uninstall removes the mesh control plane from the cluster —
    # denied outright, same reasoning as helm's uninstall above.
    istioctl:
      denied:
        - uninstall
    # Pulumi: same IaC risk profile as terraform above — `destroy` tears
    # down a stack's real infrastructure.
    pulumi:
      denied:
        - destroy
    # Packer only builds new machine images; it has no subcommand that
    # destroys existing infrastructure, so no denial rule is needed.
    # sops encrypts/decrypts files in place; it has no delete concept, so
    # no denial rule is needed — confidentiality of decrypted output is a
    # different concern than the irreversible-action governance this file
    # is for.
